equivalents.note: The Tibetan names the melody rnga bo che, 'great drum', apparently reading Bhairavī as bherī, 'kettledrum'; since rnga bo che is also an ordinary noun it is marked likely.

The Tibetan has rgyal mtshan, 'banner', and its comment (cp.12.m2) quotes the word as rgyal, 'victory', explaining victory over the seven faults that obscure samādhi as non-apprehension (dmigs pa med).

Where the Bengali has uesa (upadeśa), the Tibetan has phan thabs, 'beneficial means', matching its rendering of Munidatta's upakārikopadeśena as phan par byed pa po'i thabs (cp.12.m3), though elsewhere in the comment it renders upadeśa as man ngag.
The comment (cp.12.m5) quotes blo yis and explains it with blo gros, 'intelligence', which is to touch the perfection of wisdom (shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin ma).

The Tibetan has bde mchog bzang, 'excellent supreme bliss', with no verb for giving, and its comment (cp.12.m6) takes bde mchog as the lemma where Munidatta has dāya, so the translators read or interpreted dāha as a word for bliss rather than a move in the game.

Where the Sanskrit has akleśavaśena, 'without the power of affliction' or 'effortlessly', the Tibetan has nyon mongs pa'i dbang gis, 'by the power of the afflictions', as if its manuscript lacked the negative a-.

In Daṛatīpāda's verse the Tibetan has bsams pa yis ni rang bzhin gnas par byed, 'by thought the nature is made to abide', where the Sanskrit has candre svabhāvasthite, 'when the moon abides in its own nature'.

equivalents.wylie: dar byed pa dang bdag tu byed pa
equivalents.note: The Tibetan pair is unusual: dar may be a slip for ngar, 'as I', and bdag tu, 'as self', may stand for bdag gir, 'as mine', which would give literal calques of ahaṃkāra and mamakāra.
Where the Sanskrit has sthirīkṛtya, 'having made steady', the Tibetan has gnas par byas nas, 'having made it stay', rather than brtan, the form the glossary already records for sthira.

questions: moon (cp.12.m3): not matched. Daṛatīpāda's verse in the Tibetan has no word for the moon: where the Sanskrit has candre svabhāvasthite, 'when the moon abides in its own nature', it has bsams pa yis ni rang bzhin gnas par byed, 'by thought the nature is made to abide', as if its manuscript read a word for thought in place of candre.

siddha (cp.12.m3): not matched. Here siddho is a participle ('accomplished through Mahāmudrā'), not the title of an adept, and the Tibetan rephrases the clause as phyag rgya chen po'i dngos grub sgrub pa'i phyir, 'in order to accomplish the siddhi of Mahāmudrā'; dngos grub renders siddhi, so I have not entered it as a form of siddha.

Commentary occurrences left to the verse lines: pihari in cp.12.m2 (the Tibetan quotes it as rgyal), thakura in cp.12.m3 and cp.12.m5 (rgyal po, rgyal por) and mati in cp.12.m5 (blo yis, glossed blo gros) use the same words as the verse lines where they are given.
